newsitem.title: USA: Faulkner once again leaves Mississippi town aghast.
newsitem.headline: Faulkner once again leaves Mississippi town aghast.

text.p: Before William Faulkner won the Nobel Prize for literature, he was shunned as a drunk and a slacker by residents of his hometown in northern Mississippi.
But now, 35 years after his death, his erstwhile neighbours want to erect a statue honouring the man who has become not only their most famous native son but also the town's No. 1 tourist attraction.
And just as before, Faulkner is mostly rubbing people the wrong way.

City officials have cajoled local business people into donating $50,000 to the project. The city has hired a sculptor, set the date of the dedication and cleared the spot on the town square where the statue is to stand.

Unfortunately, clearing the site meant cutting down a magnolia tree, which caused an outcry among local tree-lovers. In a small Mississippi town, that can be trouble enough. But then last week, Faulkner's daughter and only surviving offspring informed the Oxford Board of Aldermen she was dead set against the project.
"I am horrified about the magnolia tree and the statue," Jill Faulkner Summers said in a letter read at a public meeting packed with the author's nephews and grandchildren.
Writing from her home in Charlottesville, Virginia, she asked the city council to "please honour my father's often repeated wish for privacy, and our wish for privacy as well."

Faulkner's love of privacy was legendary in Oxford. After he died in 1962, it took the city three decades to put up a sign pointing tourists to his mansion home, "Rowan Oak," now operated as a museum by the University of Mississippi.

The statue is the pet project of Oxford Mayor John Leslie and Dr. Chester McLarty, who was the Faulkner family's physician before he retired. The mayor and McLarty handled fundraising and arranged for the site.
"I'd vote for Faulkner over a tree any day," McLarty said. "I think even a 'tree-hugger' would have a hard time arguing with that."

The statue is scheduled to be dedicated Sept. 25, which would have been the author's 100th birthday. But whether that will take place has become as much a mystery as the meaning behind some of Faulkner's famously long and convoluted sentences.

The removal of the magnolia caused tempers to flare, not least because it was cut down at dawn on a Saturday morning while university students were still away on Christmas break. Although a glorious specimen of Mississippi's state tree, it was unceremoniously hauled away to a woodchipper at a local Georgia-Pacific plant.
Protesters struck back by turning the site of the fallen tree into a shrine of opposition. They even used Faulkner's own haunting words from the story, "Delta Autumn," to condemn the project.

"This land which man has deswamped, deneutered and derivered in two generations ... no wonder the ruined woods I used to know don't cry for retribution! The people who have destroyed it will accomplish its revenge," demonstrators read aloud at one protest.
Some Faulkner buffs hoped to please everyone by proposing to have the statue erected at Rowan Oak mansion, appropriately nestled on secluded grounds a few blocks from the square.
But Faulkner's daughter showed no interest in compromise. "I do not want the statue of my father put on the square or anywhere else," she wrote in her letter.

The city does not need family approval to proceed with its plans. But as alderman David Magee put it: "We didn't want a statue that would forever be marked in history as 'the statue the family didn't want.'"
For the time being, some Faulkner relatives have agreed to join a committee to review the issue with the mayor, sculptor Bill Beckwith and three city aldermen.
